newsitem.title: UK: Britain drinking more tea but Sri Lanka loses out.
newsitem.headline: Britain drinking more tea but Sri Lanka loses out.

text.p: Sri Lankan tea has almost priced itself out of a growing British market, with the daily cuppa more likely to be an African blend such as Kenyan now.

A British obsession with quick-brewing teabags, which are less suited to the large leaf teas produced in Sri Lanka and India, is the chief underlying factor in the decline of imports from these countries, industry sources said.
"Sri Lankan tea prices have shot up way above what UK buyers are willing to pay," Robin Harrison of the UK Tea Brokers Association said.
Meanwhile, Kenya increased its share of British imports by 30 percent during the first six months of 1996, but Sri Lankan imports fell by 20 percent to around 5,000 tons, Association figures show.
Sri Lanka now has just seven percent of the recovering UK import market while Kenya has 57 percent.
Blenders are tending to prefer Indian to Sri Lankan tea to add quality to their blends, although Indian teas are also losing favour due to high prices, one source said.
However, Indian tea has maintained its share of British imports at around 15 percent.
Sri Lankan and Indian tea is mostly used in the speciality teas which currently hold 7-9 percent of the UK retail market.
"There are no indications that this will change," a UK Tea Council spokesman said.
This also means that Britain will not be particularly affected by the projected increase in South Asian production, as African tea now accounts for 72 percent of UK imports.
Total British tea imports rose ten percent to 88,000 tons in the first six months of 1996.
Prices have risen as well, and at the most recent UK tea auction on September 9 were 10-15 pct above the same period last year.
The market had been oversupplied, with average auction prices for landed teas reaching historical lows of around 100/102 pence per kg in 1995.
But de-stocking masked the fact that overall demand actually increased by five percent in 1995, said Harrison.
This is good news for British packers and blenders who built up their stocks while prices were low, looking for a recovery in demand, he said.
"They're now beginning to buy the raw material again," Harrison said.
The Tea Council spokesman was hoping for a repeat of 1995's summer when retail tea sales were unseasonably high.
"Demand appeared to be holding up until March this year so it is looking good for the summer figures", he said.
